pedagogy.summary: Collecting like terms means combining terms that share the SAME letter AND the same power, keeping each term's sign, and leaving unlike terms uncombined. The deep obstacle is not the procedure but 'acceptance of lack of closure' (Collis): children see 3a + 2b as an instruction to be finished rather than an answer in its own right, so they force it closed — conjoining to 5ab, or reaching for a single number. Teach it as sorting a mixed pile into groups, using quantities ('the number of a's') rather than objects, and make explicit that a fully-simplified expression can be several terms.
bestPractices: Treat collecting as sorting: group a-terms, b-terms and constants separately; only terms in the same group combine.
Insist on same letter AND same power — 3a and 2a² are NOT like terms; contrast a (length) with a² (area).
Keep each term's sign attached to it: in 4a − b + 2a, the − belongs to the b; collect signed coefficients.
Directly confront lack of closure: rehearse that 3a + 2b IS the answer and cannot be made shorter — an expression is an object, not an unfinished sum.
Prefer 'number of apples' over 'a = apple': the object/fruit-salad analogy breeds the letter-as-object error and licenses conjoining (a+b='ab').
keyRepresentations: Algebra tiles (an x-tile, a y-tile, a unit tile — only identical tiles stack)
Sorting groups / columns by term type
Area square for a² vs a bar for a (why powers differ)
commonMisconceptions: Conjoins unlike terms to 'close' the expression: 3a + 2b → 5ab or one number, because an open sum feels unfinished (lack of closure, Collis).
Combines terms with the same letter but different powers: 3a + 2a² → 5a² or 5a³.
Loses or mishandles a sign when collecting: treats −b as +b, or 5a − 3a as 8a.
Drops the variable when combining: 3a + 5a → 8 instead of 8a.
Letter-as-object thinking (a = apple) that makes a + b feel like it should be 'ab'.

learn.summary: Collecting like terms means combining only terms that share the SAME letter AND the same power, keeping each term's sign, and leaving unlike terms uncombined. The deep obstacle is 'acceptance of lack of closure' (Collis): learners treat 3a + 2b as an instruction to be finished rather than as an answer in its own right, so they force it closed by conjoining to 5ab or reaching for a single number. Teach collecting as sorting a mixed pile into groups, talk in quantities ('the number of a's') rather than objects, and make explicit that a fully-simplified expression can be several terms.

activities.title: The sort that refuses to merge (algebra-tile bench)
feedback: If a learner forces an a-tile onto a b-tile, point to the refusal: different tiles cannot pool, so 3a + 2b stays as two terms.
When three tidy stacks remain, confirm explicitly: '3a + 2b + 5 is finished — it does not need to become one number or one term.'
In negative mode, if a red tile is ignored, show the cancellation: one anti-b removes one b, so 3b − b = 2b, not 4b.
activities.rationale: Tiles that physically refuse to combine give a concrete counter to the closure urge, and sorting mirrors the 'group a-terms, b-terms and constants' structure of the procedure. A manipulative lets learners rehearse the comparison directly; this is a proposed design, not evidence that tiles outperform other media.
sourceClaims: Children are reluctant to 'accept lack of closure' (Collis): asked what e+f+g is when e+f=8, only ~41% of Year 9 gave 8+g in 1976 and there was no improvement 30 years later; interviews show '8g' feels like a finished answer while '8+g' feels like an unfinished sum to be worked out — the drive that produces conjoining.
learnerActions: Start with a jumbled heap of a-tiles, b-tiles and unit-tiles mixed together.
Drag identical tiles together so they stack and label themselves (three a-tiles become '3a', two b-tiles become '2b', five unit-tiles become '5').
Deliberately try to press an a-tile onto a b-tile — notice it will not fuse and springs apart; you cannot build an 'ab' tile this way.
State the finished result as three separate stacks: 3a, 2b, 5, and say aloud that this is fully simplified.
Switch on a negative-coefficient mode where red 'anti-tiles' cancel matching tiles, e.g. show how 3b − b leaves 2b.
activities.intendedInsight: Unlike terms genuinely cannot be merged, and the leftover collection of separate terms IS the complete answer — an expression is an object, not an unfinished sum.

activities.title: Sort and complete the expression
feedback: If 'a' and '2b' land in the same bin, remind: same letter AND same power required to share a group.
If 5ab is chosen, respond that a-terms and b-terms are different piles and cannot pool — the answer keeps both.
If the − is dropped from 2b, re-attach the sign to its term before combining.
activities.rationale: A categorisation and completion check surfaces conjoining and sign errors through learners' own responses. This response format can both assess and, used while teaching, rehearse the sort; recognising a correct form does not by itself show a learner can independently construct a simplified expression, so learner-produced simplifications are also required.
learnerActions: Drag each term of 4a − 2b + 3 + a into the correct bin: 'a-terms', 'b-terms', or 'numbers' (the − stays attached to the 2b).
Choose the correct simplified form from options that include the closure-driven trap '5ab' and a sign-error option — and give a one-line reason for rejecting 5ab.
activities.intendedInsight: Correctly sorted, signed terms simplify to several terms; conjoining to a single term or number is wrong, and each sign travels with its own term.

activities.title: Name the parts of a term
feedback: If a learner groups a with a², contrast the bar (length a) with the square (area a²): visibly different objects that do not combine.
Prefer 'the number of a's' over 'a = apple'; the object analogy encourages a + b feeling like it should be 'ab'.
activities.rationale: A labelled, tappable reference builds term vocabulary and the length-vs-area contrast for powers. It is a glossary scaffold: because the example is fixed it cannot be rearranged by the learner, so it does not elicit independent sorting — pair it with the construction activities.
sourceClaims: Letter-as-object interpretations of algebraic letters (a = apple), which license conjoining unlike terms, are a long-documented CSMS-tradition difficulty among secondary students.
learnerActions: Given a pre-sorted expression such as 3a + 2b + 5, tap each term to reveal its type (a-term, b-term, constant) and its signed coefficient.
Say in words what each term counts: 'the number of a's is 3', 'the number of b's is 2', '5 is a constant on its own'.
Explain why 2a and a² are different terms: a can stand for a length (a bar) and a² for an area (a square), so they are different objects and 3a + 2a² cannot be collected.
activities.intendedInsight: The vocabulary of terms, coefficients and powers, and why same-letter-different-power terms (a vs a²) are unlike and cannot pool.

activities.title: Confront lack of closure in words
feedback: If a learner insists on one number, affirm that 6a + 2b + 5 is itself the answer — there is nothing further to do.

If 7ab is accepted, talk in quantities: the number of a's (4) and the number of b's (3) stay in different groups. Substituting a = 2, b = 5 gives 23 for 4a + 3b but 70 for 7ab, so they are not equivalent.
If the − is attached to the wrong term, re-read 4a − b + 2a as 'take away one b', so the b-total is −b and the result is 6a − b.
activities.rationale: Explicit discussion targets the closure belief head-on and rehearses sign handling, which a silent sort may leave implicit. Discussion is one route to articulating the reasoning and complements the manipulative; it is not claimed here to be more effective than other media.
sourceClaims: Children are reluctant to 'accept lack of closure' (Collis): asked what e+f+g is when e+f=8, only ~41% of Year 9 gave 8+g in 1976 and there was no improvement 30 years later; interviews show '8g' feels like a finished answer while '8+g' feels like an unfinished sum to be worked out — the drive that produces conjoining.
learnerActions: Decide whether 6a + 2b + 5 is finished or whether there should be a single number at the end, and explain how you know.

Answer: is 4a + 3b equivalent to 7ab, meaning equal for every value of a and b? Test a = 2, b = 5 (23 vs 70) and explain why they are not equivalent, even though a few special values (such as a = b = 1) happen to give equal numbers.
Use quantity language to test conjoining: say 'the number of a's is 4 and the number of b's is 3', then explain why these two counts stay separate instead of becoming 7 of a new thing called 'ab'.
Track a sign: in 4a − b + 2a, say where the minus sign belongs and simplify (answer: 6a − b).
activities.intendedInsight: A multi-term expression can be the complete answer; conjoining unlike terms is never valid, and each sign belongs to its own term.

constraints: Insist on same letter AND same power: 3a and 2a² are not like terms; contrast a (length) with a² (area).
Keep each term's sign attached before combining: in 4a − b + 2a the − belongs to the b; collect signed coefficients.
Prefer 'the number of a's' over 'a = apple'; the object/fruit-salad analogy breeds letter-as-object thinking and licenses conjoining (a + b = 'ab').
Make explicit that a fully-simplified expression can be several terms — an expression is an object, not an unfinished instruction.

The tap-to-reveal labelled expression is a vocabulary scaffold: its fixed example cannot be rearranged by the learner, so it does not elicit independent sorting or construction. Pair it with tasks where learners build and sort.

The categorisation/selection check uses recognition and selection; recognising a correct form does not guarantee a learner can independently construct a simplified expression, so also require learner-produced simplifications.
Algebra tiles and discussion offer different experiences (manipulation vs articulation); neither is claimed here to be the only way to fix the closure misconception.
Watch written working rather than only final answers: a merged single term, a wrong sign, or a dropped variable each show as a distinct final line.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. The activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

The original source row asserted the tile 'directly defeats the closure urge', that a third spatial dimension 'adds nothing', and that a static image 'cannot stage' the merge experience. These are catalog-style comparative/necessity claims not established by the cited sources; they have been softened to scoped proposals with stated affordances and limits.

The Küchemann/Hart CSMS claim is marked verified:false in the source and should be checked before relying on it; the two DfE and Hodgen et al. claims are marked verified:true in the legacy data but were not re-verified in this rewrite.

The source row's own error examples '5a − 3a as 8a' and '3a + 5a → 8' are listed as misconceptions to detect, not as correct arithmetic; correct values are 5a − 3a = 2a and 3a + 5a = 8a. These appear only in diagnostic/feedback framing, never as valid learner answers.

The KS3 DfE claim is a topic/curriculum statement and does not directly support any activity's teaching-principle rationale, so it is not attached as sourceClaims to the tile or sort activities; the scored-sort activity likewise has sourceClaims set to [].

probeDeeper: Is 6a + 2b + 5 finished, or should there be a single number at the end? How do you know? (probes lack of closure head-on)
Could 4a + 3b ever be written as 7ab? If so, when — if never, why not? (counterexample confronting conjoining)
What is the difference between 2a and a² — and can you collect 3a + 2a²? (powers)
When you dealt with − b, where did the minus sign go, and why?
assess.correctAnswer: 6a + 2b + 5. (4a + 2a = 6a; 3b − b = 2b; the 5 is a constant on its own; nothing else combines.)

errorPatterns.pattern: Conjoins unlike terms to force closure — '3a + 2b must make 5ab' or 'there has to be a proper answer' — because an open expression feels unfinished (documented: only ~41% of Year 9 accept e+f+g = 8+g; 'ab feels finished, a+b feels like an unfinished sum').
errorPatterns.nextMove: Use a quantities context (4 apples + 3 bananas is not '7 abananas') and tiles that refuse to merge; establish explicitly that 6a + 2b + 5 IS the answer — an expression can be an object, not an instruction.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Merges a-terms and b-terms into a single term (5ab), or insists on reducing to one number; says the expression 'isn't finished' until it is one item.

errorPatterns.pattern: Combines same-letter, different-power terms — treats 3a and 2a² as like, giving 5a² or 5a³.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Like terms need the SAME letter AND the same power; contrast a (a bar) with a² (a square) so they are visibly different objects that cannot pool.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Adds coefficients of a and a² together; groups a with a² when sorting.

errorPatterns.pattern: Loses a sign when collecting — reads −b as +b, or mishandles a negative coefficient, e.g. 3b − b → 4b.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Do not reteach collecting — attach each sign to its own term first (the − belongs to the b), then combine signed coefficients; rehearse directed-number addition in place.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: The sign attached to a term is dropped or flipped in the working; b-total comes out too large.

responseLevels.gap: Merges unlike terms into one term or a single number, or cannot begin; treats the expression as a sum to be 'worked out' to one answer.
responseLevels.full: Collects a-terms, b-terms and constants separately with correct signs, leaves the answer as several terms without unease (accepts lack of closure), rejects 3a+2b=5ab with a reason, and transfers to unfamiliar variables and powers.
responseLevels.partial: Collects like terms correctly when coefficients are positive and single-variable, but slips on the negative term, on the lone constant, or on same-letter-different-power — combines the parts it recognises but not reliably, and may still be uneasy leaving several terms.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Hand the child this card and say 'simplify this as far as you can, showing your working': 4a + 3b + 2a − b + 5. Say nothing about method. Watch whether they keep a-terms, b-terms and the constant separate, how they treat the −b, and whether they try to force everything into a single term.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: Because the teacher watches the written working rather than asking, each error shows as a different final line: a child driven to close writes one merged term (e.g. 15ab, or a single number); a child who mishandles the sign gets 4b instead of 2b; a child who drops variables gets a bare number; a sound child leaves three separate terms with correct signs and shows no unease that the answer 'isn't one number'.
